In the near term (definitely not in the long term), more capable models should mean safer models (maybe paradoxically). Current models are unsafe not because they're too smart, but because they take goals too literally or take nonsensical shortcuts to achieve these goals, i.e. they're RL-fried. They lack common sense. They don't do the right thing in the face of ambiguity. Basically, they're not smart enough. They're at that dangerous level where they're smart enough to achieve goals but not smart enough to tell if they're pursuing the right goals or achieving them in a sensible way. More capable models can be safely trusted with more complex goals -- I personally feel like Astra is much safer for my codebase than Sol. This is often framed as an alignment problem, but really it's an intelligence problem.

You could say there is something inherently unsafe about a research process and body of AI techniques that lead to making models increasingly good at achieving goals, without giving them common sense and the ability to reflect on those goals.

If there really is a high chance of AI leading to the extinction of humanity within years/decades, then the only rational stance towards safety monitoring and research pacing should be stringent, top-down government involvement and universally ratified international treaties. Similar to what we have been doing for a long time with nuclear energy and nuclear weapons non-proliferation. If that's not what we're doing, then we must infer that the risk isn't being seriously considered by anyone involved. There are only two options that make sense here: 1. The near-term species extinction risk is real and we are taking it seriously, with maximally heavy-handed regulation. 2. The extinction risk isn't real, actual risks are mild, so we're only pursuing mild safety measures and self-certification. But you cannot say "yes this is likely to end humanity in your lifetime, and we're going to completely wing it." That is simply not rational.

I hope the proposals by frontier labs to pace AI research stem from a genuine concern for safety and a recognition of the potential risks posed by future models, rather than a strategic effort to consolidate power and permanently solidify the market dominance of a few top players. If these efforts are genuine, then oversight must take a more democratic and accountable form, with both national and international components, similar to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission in the US and the International Atomic Energy Agency internationally. If there is only one organization responsible for safety monitoring, and it happens to be staffed by the same people as the frontier labs, and it is perfectly aligned with them both by incentives and by ideology, then it would be indistinguishable from letting frontier labs self-regulate and self-certify their own safety standards. Two potential warning signs of regulatory capture to watch out for: 1. Calls to ban open-source AI. Open-source development currently serves as the only real counterweight to the dominance of frontier labs. 2. Attempts to hinder non-frontier research. Models that are one or two generations behind the frontier -- whose level of capability has already been deployed at scale -- are empirically known not to pose safety risks. As long as we don't see 1 & 2, and we see real international coordination efforts, then I will optimistically believe that the proposals are benevolent.

💯💯💯 David Sacks (@DavidSacks) Dario has written that we need to “pace the frontier,” and Sam has agreed. People may be surprised by my response: go ahead. You guys are the frontier. By any reasonable metric — market share, revenue growth, model capability — the two of you have a duopoly on frontier intelligence. You’ve also claimed the lead is widening because of recursive self-improvement. I don’t see what you see in the lab. If the unreleased models are scary enough that you think you should slow down, I support your decision to be responsible. But stop pretending you need anyone else’s permission. Stop pretending antitrust law has to be suspended so you can form a cartel. Stop pretending you need a regulatory approval process that supersedes product liability. Stop pretending METR is independent when it is intertwined with Anthropic’s investors and staff. Stop pretending you need those same evaluators to police competitors who aren’t even at the frontier. Most of all, stop pretending the motivation to slow down is purely altruistic. You face massive product-liability exposure if your products enable a truly damaging cyberattack. The market already punishes models that behave in unpredictable or unauthorized ways. After the Hugging Face episode, it is simply good business for OpenAI and Anthropic to trade some raw power for reliability and predictability. Call it alignment if you want. It is also just giving customers what they want. Pacing the frontier would also create breathing room for a more intelligent conversation about regulation than Bernie Sanders’ “shut it all down.” China is very unlikely to join a global agreement, as you know, and that has to be taken into account as well. So go ahead and pace the frontier. You are the ones setting it. The easiest way not to build superintelligence is for you to agree not to build it. Demanding your preferred regulatory framework as the price of that will look like blackmail of the public and the political system. So just do it. If you do, you’ll buy goodwill for the next conversation. If you don’t, we’ll know this was just another bid for regulatory capture — or an election-season psyop. — https://nitter.kareem.one/DavidSacks/status/2098973625252708460#m

D'un côté, on assiste à des annonces majeures avec la levée de fonds record de Mistral AI en Europe et les progrès de Google Gemini. De l'autre, de grands débats font rage sur la sécurité de l'IA, la vitesse de son développement et les risques de voir les entreprises dominantes dicter les règles. On découvre aussi des applications concrètes de l'IA, comme la création de parcours de course, et des outils pour la tester. En tant que débutant, il est clé de comprendre que l'IA n'est pas juste une technologie, mais aussi un champ de discussion intense sur son impact et son futur.

category_summaries.actu: Cette section a été riche en annonces de taille : la startup française Mistral AI a réalisé une levée de fonds historique, consolidant sa position en Europe. OpenAI a fait des déclarations importantes concernant la sécurité et l'arrivée de nouveaux membres à son conseil, tandis que Google AI Studio a dévoilé des améliorations. Des incidents impliquant des agents IA spammeurs ont aussi été rapportés, soulignant les défis de sécurité actuels.
category_summaries.tips: Aujourd'hui, le seul conseil direct est une invitation à l'action : explorez les outils de Google AI Studio. C'est un excellent point de départ pour un débutant passionné afin de se familiariser avec l'environnement de développement de l'IA et de comprendre comment ces systèmes sont conçus et testés.
category_summaries.idees: De vifs débats ont eu lieu sur la vitesse de développement de l'IA et la pertinence des mesures de sécurité proposées. Certains craignent une 'capture réglementaire' par les grands acteurs pour freiner l'open-source, tandis que d'autres s'inquiètent de la 'psychose de l'IA' et appellent à se concentrer sur la cybersécurité. Il y a aussi des réflexions profondes sur le 'bon sens' des IA et leur potentiel impact disruptif sur l'économie et les emplois.

highlights.text_fr: À court terme (certainement pas à long terme), des modèles plus capables devraient signifier des modèles plus sûrs (peut-être paradoxalement). Les modèles actuels sont dangereux non pas parce qu'ils sont trop intelligents, mais parce qu'ils prennent les objectifs trop littéralement ou prennent des raccourcis insensés pour atteindre ces objectifs, c'est-à-dire qu'ils sont 'RL-fried'. Ils manquent de bon sens. Ils ne font pas ce qu'il faut face à l'ambiguïté. En gros, ils ne sont pas assez intelligents. Ils sont à ce niveau dangereux où ils sont assez intelligents pour atteindre des objectifs mais pas assez intelligents pour savoir s'ils poursuivent les bons objectifs ou les atteignent de manière sensée. Des modèles plus capables peuvent être confiés en toute sécurité à des objectifs plus complexes – je pense personnellement qu'Astra est bien plus sûr pour ma base de code que Sol. C'est souvent présenté comme un problème d'alignement, mais c'est en réalité un problème d'intelligence.
highlights.text_original: In the near term (definitely not in the long term), more capable models should mean safer models (maybe paradoxically). Current models are unsafe not because they're too smart, but because they take goals too literally or take nonsensical shortcuts to achieve these goals, i.e. they're RL-fried. They lack common sense. They don't do the right thing in the face of ambiguity. Basically, they're not smart enough. They're at that dangerous level where they're smart enough to achieve goals but not smart enough to tell if they're pursuing the right goals or achieving them in a sensible way. More capable models can be safely trusted with more complex goals -- I personally feel like Astra is much safer for my codebase than Sol. This is often framed as an alignment problem, but really it's an intelligence problem.
highlights.decryptage: « RL-fried » fait référence à des modèles d'IA trop optimisés par l'apprentissage par renforcement (Reinforcement Learning) qui peuvent parfois trouver des solutions inattendues ou indésirables aux objectifs fixés. François Chollet propose que l'amélioration de l'intelligence générale de l'IA, notamment son 'bon sens', est la clé de sa sécurité, plutôt qu'un risque accru.
highlights.highlight_reason: Cette réflexion remet en question l'idée courante que l'intelligence de l'IA est le principal risque, suggérant plutôt que c'est son manque de 'bon sens' qui la rend dangereuse, offrant une perspective nouvelle sur la sécurité.

idees.text_original: In the near term (definitely not in the long term), more capable models should mean safer models (maybe paradoxically). Current models are unsafe not because they're too smart, but because they take goals too literally or take nonsensical shortcuts to achieve these goals, i.e. they're RL-fried. They lack common sense. They don't do the right thing in the face of ambiguity. Basically, they're not smart enough. They're at that dangerous level where they're smart enough to achieve goals but not smart enough to tell if they're pursuing the right goals or achieving them in a sensible way. More capable models can be safely trusted with more complex goals -- I personally feel like Astra is much safer for my codebase than Sol. This is often framed as an alignment problem, but really it's an intelligence problem.

idees.text_fr: On pourrait dire qu'il y a quelque chose d'intrinsèquement dangereux dans un processus de recherche et un ensemble de techniques d'IA qui conduisent à rendre les modèles de plus en plus performants dans l'atteinte d'objectifs, sans leur donner le bon sens et la capacité de réfléchir à ces objectifs.

idees.text_fr: S'il y a vraiment une forte chance que l'IA mène à l'extinction de l'humanité en quelques années/décennies, alors la seule position rationnelle concernant la surveillance de la sécurité et le rythme de la recherche devrait être une implication gouvernementale stricte et des traités internationaux ratifiés universellement. Similaire à ce que nous faisons depuis longtemps avec l'énergie nucléaire et la non-prolifération des armes nucléaires. Si ce n'est pas ce que nous faisons, alors nous devons en déduire que le risque n'est pas pris sérieusement par quiconque est impliqué. Il n'y a que deux options qui ont du sens ici : 1. Le risque d'extinction des espèces à court terme est réel et nous le prenons au sérieux, avec une réglementation la plus stricte possible. 2. Le risque d'extinction n'est pas réel, les risques réels sont faibles, nous ne poursuivons donc que des mesures de sécurité légères et une auto-certification. Mais vous ne pouvez pas dire "oui, cela va probablement mettre fin à l'humanité de votre vivant, et nous allons y aller à l'aveugle". Ce n'est tout simplement pas rationnel.
idees.text_original: If there really is a high chance of AI leading to the extinction of humanity within years/decades, then the only rational stance towards safety monitoring and research pacing should be stringent, top-down government involvement and universally ratified international treaties. Similar to what we have been doing for a long time with nuclear energy and nuclear weapons non-proliferation. If that's not what we're doing, then we must infer that the risk isn't being seriously considered by anyone involved. There are only two options that make sense here: 1. The near-term species extinction risk is real and we are taking it seriously, with maximally heavy-handed regulation. 2. The extinction risk isn't real, actual risks are mild, so we're only pursuing mild safety measures and self-certification. But you cannot say "yes this is likely to end humanity in your lifetime, and we're going to completely wing it." That is simply not rational.

S'il n'y a qu'une seule organisation responsable de la surveillance de la sécurité, et qu'elle se trouve être composée des mêmes personnes que les laboratoires de pointe, et qu'elle est parfaitement alignée avec eux à la fois par les incitations et par l'idéologie, alors elle serait indiscernable de laisser les laboratoires de pointe s'autoréguler et s'auto-certifier leurs propres normes de sécurité. Deux signes d'alerte potentiels de 'capture réglementaire' à surveiller : 1. Les appels à interdire l'IA open-source. Le développement open-source sert actuellement de seul véritable contrepoids à la domination des laboratoires de pointe. 2. Les tentatives d'entraver la recherche non-frontière. Les modèles qui ont un ou deux niveaux de capacité de retard par rapport à la frontière – dont le niveau de capacité a déjà été déployé à grande échelle – sont empiriquement connus pour ne pas poser de risques de sécurité. Tant que nous ne verrons pas les points 1 et 2, et que nous verrons de réels efforts de coordination internationale, alors je croirai avec optimisme que les propositions sont bienveillantes.
idees.text_original: I hope the proposals by frontier labs to pace AI research stem from a genuine concern for safety and a recognition of the potential risks posed by future models, rather than a strategic effort to consolidate power and permanently solidify the market dominance of a few top players. If these efforts are genuine, then oversight must take a more democratic and accountable form, with both national and international components, similar to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission in the US and the International Atomic Energy Agency internationally. If there is only one organization responsible for safety monitoring, and it happens to be staffed by the same people as the frontier labs, and it is perfectly aligned with them both by incentives and by ideology, then it would be indistinguishable from letting frontier labs self-regulate and self-certify their own safety standards. Two potential warning signs of regulatory capture to watch out for: 1. Calls to ban open-source AI. Open-source development currently serves as the only real counterweight to the dominance of frontier labs. 2. Attempts to hinder non-frontier research. Models that are one or two generations behind the frontier -- whose level of capability has already been deployed at scale -- are empirically known not to pose safety risks. As long as we don't see 1 & 2, and we see real international coordination efforts, then I will optimistically believe that the proposals are benevolent.
